name: Lymphatic and immune system
description: Lymph, lymphatic vessels and nodes, the spleen, thymus, tonsils and other lymphoid tissue, and how the innate and adaptive immune system defends the body: white cells, antibodies, vaccines, allergy and autoimmunity. Pictures show the spleen, thymus and appendix to name; BodyParts3D has no model of the lymph nodes or vessels, so the rest is text questions.

source.name: Written for Study Buddy. Pictures rendered from BodyParts3D (© The Database Center for Life Science, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP).

questions.prompt: What are the main parts of the lymphatic system?
answers: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, lymph nodes and lymphoid organs
Lymphatic vessels, lymph nodes, spleen, thymus and tonsils
wrong: Bone marrow, blood and the liver only
questions.explanation: Together they drain tissue fluid, absorb fats and defend the body.

questions.prompt: What is lymph?
answers: Tissue fluid that has entered lymphatic vessels
Clear fluid, much like plasma, carried in lymphatic vessels
wrong: Blood without red cells, carried in the arteries
A fluid made by the lymph nodes
questions.explanation: About 3 litres a day return to the blood this way.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a function of the lymphatic system?
wrong: Returning tissue fluid to the blood
questions.explanation: Red blood cells carry oxygen.

questions.prompt: How do lymphatic capillaries differ from blood capillaries?
answers: They are blind-ended and very leaky, so fluid and large particles can get in
They start as closed-ended tubes with loosely overlapping cells
wrong: They carry blood to the veins
They are joined to the arteries
questions.explanation: Flaps between the cells work as one-way valves.

questions.prompt: What makes lymph flow towards the heart?
answers: Movement of the skeletal muscles and breathing, with valves in the vessels
Skeletal muscle pump, breathing and one-way valves
wrong: A pump in the lymph nodes
questions.explanation: There is no heart for the lymph.

questions.prompt: What are the lymphatic capillaries in the villi of the small intestine, which absorb fats, called?
questions.explanation: The lymph is milky from the fats, and is called chyle.

questions.prompt: What is the milky lymph from the intestine, full of absorbed fat, called?
questions.explanation: Not to be confused with chyme, the semi-digested food in the stomach.

questions.prompt: Which large lymph duct drains the left side of the head, neck and chest and everything below the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: It empties into the left subclavian vein, where it meets the left internal jugular vein.

questions.prompt: Which part of the body does the right lymphatic duct drain?
answers: The right side of the head, neck and chest, and the right arm
The upper right quarter of the body
wrong: The whole body below the diaphragm
questions.explanation: It empties into the right subclavian vein.

questions.prompt: What is the sac at the lower end of the thoracic duct, in the abdomen, called?
questions.explanation: It gathers lymph from the legs and the intestines.

questions.prompt: Where are lymph nodes found in clusters that you can feel when they swell?
questions.explanation: Others are deep, such as in the chest and abdomen.

questions.prompt: What shape and size is a typical lymph node?
questions.explanation: The lymph enters through several afferent vessels, and leaves through one efferent vessel at the hilum.

questions.prompt: Which lymph vessels carry lymph into a node, and which carry it out?
answers: Afferent vessels bring it in; efferent vessels take it away
wrong: Lymph enters through the hilum only
questions.explanation: There are more afferent than efferent vessels, which slows the flow through the node.

questions.prompt: What do lymph nodes do?
answers: They filter lymph and are where the immune response is started
Filter lymph and house lymphocytes and macrophages
wrong: They pump lymph to the heart
They make red blood cells in adults
questions.explanation: Macrophages remove germs, and B and T cells are activated.

questions.prompt: Why do lymph nodes swell during an infection?
answers: Lymphocytes divide to fight the germs
wrong: The vessels are blocked by fat
questions.explanation: They are usually tender. A hard, painless node needs checking for cancer.

questions.prompt: What is the swelling of a limb caused by blocked or removed lymph vessels, for example after removal of nodes, called?
questions.explanation: The fluid cannot drain.

questions.prompt: Why do doctors check the lymph nodes near a cancer?
answers: Cancer cells often spread through the lymph to the nodes
To see if cancer has spread through the lymph
wrong: Nodes hold a lot of blood
questions.explanation: The first node reached is called the sentinel node.

questions.prompt: Which organ is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The largest lymphoid organ, under the diaphragm at the left of the stomach, protected by the lower ribs.

figure.alt: The spleen, in red, on the left of the upper abdomen
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: What are the main jobs of the spleen?
answers: It filters old red cells from the blood and holds lymphocytes to fight infection
Filtering blood, removing old red cells, immune response
questions.explanation: The red pulp filters, the white pulp is lymphoid tissue.

figure.alt: The spleen, in red, on the left of the upper abdomen
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Does the spleen filter lymph or blood?
questions.explanation: Unlike the lymph nodes, it has no afferent lymph vessels.

questions.prompt: Why are people without a spleen given vaccines against encapsulated bacteria?
answers: They are more likely to get severe infections with them
Without the spleen, they are at risk of overwhelming infections
questions.explanation: Such as pneumococcus.

questions.prompt: Which gland is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Where T cells mature. It is biggest in childhood and shrinks after puberty.

figure.alt: The thymus behind the sternum, in red, with the rib cage drawn see-through
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which lymphoid tissue, a ring around the throat, guards the entrance to the airways and gut?
questions.explanation: The palatine tonsils are the ones seen at the back of the mouth. The adenoids are the pharyngeal tonsil.

questions.prompt: Which tonsil sits at the back of the nose?
What are the clusters of lymphoid tissue in the wall of the ileum called?
questions.explanation: They sample what is in the gut.

questions.prompt: Which structure is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: A small blind tube off the caecum, rich in lymphoid tissue.

figure.alt: The appendix, in red, at the start of the large intestine
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: What is the name for the scattered lymphoid tissue in the gut, airways and other mucosa?
questions.explanation: It is where most of the body's lymphocytes are.

questions.prompt: Where are all the blood cells, including lymphocytes, made?
questions.explanation: The B cells mature there. The T cells mature in the thymus.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between innate and adaptive immunity?
answers: Innate responds the same way to every germ at once; adaptive is specific and remembers
Innate is quick and general; adaptive is slow, specific and has memory
wrong: Innate is specific and has memory; adaptive is general
questions.explanation: The skin and phagocytes are innate. B and T cells are adaptive.

questions.prompt: Which of these is part of the body's first line of defence?
questions.explanation: Also acid in the stomach, tears with lysozyme, and cilia in the airways.

questions.prompt: Which type of white blood cell is the most common?
questions.explanation: 40 to 70% of white cells. They are the first to arrive at an infection.

questions.prompt: What is the process of cells engulfing and digesting germs called?
questions.explanation: Done by neutrophils and macrophages.

questions.prompt: Which cell, formed from a monocyte in the tissues, engulfs germs and shows pieces of them to T cells?
questions.explanation: That makes it an antigen-presenting cell.

questions.prompt: Which lymphocytes attack virus-infected cells and tumour cells without first being sensitised?
questions.explanation: They are part of the innate defence.

questions.prompt: Which white cells fight parasites such as worms and are raised in allergy?
Which four signs mark acute inflammation?
questions.explanation: Loss of function is sometimes added as a fifth.

questions.prompt: Which chemical, released by mast cells, widens the blood vessels and makes them leaky in inflammation and allergy?
questions.explanation: Antihistamines block it.

questions.prompt: How does a fever help fight infection?
answers: It slows many germs and speeds up the immune response
It makes the body less good for germs
questions.explanation: It is set by the hypothalamus in response to pyrogens.

questions.prompt: Which proteins, released by virus-infected cells, warn their neighbours to resist the virus?
What is the name for the group of blood proteins that punch holes in germs and mark them for phagocytes?
questions.explanation: Over 30 proteins.

questions.prompt: What is an antigen?
answers: A molecule that triggers an immune response
A substance the immune system recognises as foreign
questions.explanation: Often a protein or sugar on a germ's surface.

questions.prompt: Which lymphocytes make antibodies?
questions.explanation: A B cell that meets its antigen turns into antibody-producing plasma cells and memory cells.

questions.prompt: Which lymphocytes mature in the thymus?
questions.explanation: The T stands for thymus.

questions.prompt: Which T cells, carrying CD4, help the other immune cells by releasing cytokines? They are the cells HIV destroys.
questions.explanation: HIV infects them, so the immune system collapses in AIDS.

questions.prompt: Which T cells, carrying CD8, kill infected and cancer cells?
What shape is an antibody (immunoglobulin) molecule?
questions.explanation: It has two identical antigen-binding sites at the tips.

questions.prompt: Which antibody class is the most common in the blood and the only one to cross the placenta?
questions.explanation: It protects the newborn for the first months.

questions.prompt: Which antibody class is found in tears, saliva, milk and mucus?
questions.explanation: Passed in breast milk, it protects the baby's gut.

questions.prompt: Which antibody class is made first in a new infection?
questions.explanation: A big pentamer.

questions.prompt: Which antibody class is behind allergies and defence against parasites?
questions.explanation: It sits on mast cells and makes them release histamine.

questions.prompt: Why is the second response to the same germ faster and stronger than the first?
answers: Memory cells from the first exposure
Because memory B and T cells were made
wrong: The body has more white cells
The antibodies from before are still there in full
questions.explanation: This is the basis of vaccination.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between active and passive immunity?
answers: In active immunity the body makes its own antibodies; in passive immunity it is given them
Active means you make your own; passive means they are given to you
wrong: Active is short-lived; passive is lifelong
questions.explanation: Passive: antibodies across the placenta, in milk or by injection. They last only weeks to months.

questions.prompt: How does a vaccine give protection?
answers: It shows the immune system an antigen so that it makes memory cells without causing the disease
It makes memory cells, without the illness
wrong: It kills germs in the blood
questions.explanation: That is active, artificial immunity.

questions.prompt: What is herd immunity?
answers: When enough people are immune that the disease cannot spread easily
Protection of the unvaccinated because most are immune
wrong: When the whole herd gets ill together

questions.prompt: What is an allergy?
answers: An over-reaction of the immune system to a harmless antigen
An exaggerated immune response to something harmless
wrong: A reaction to a vaccine only
questions.explanation: Typical allergens are pollen, nuts and dust mites.

questions.prompt: What is a severe, sudden, life-threatening allergic reaction called?
questions.explanation: Treated at once with adrenaline.

questions.prompt: What is an autoimmune disease?
answers: The immune system attacks the body's own tissue
wrong: The immune system is too weak
A cancer of the immune system
questions.explanation: Examples: type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis.

questions.prompt: What does HIV do to the body?
answers: It destroys helper T cells, so the immune system weakens
questions.explanation: In AIDS, the person has serious infections and some cancers.

questions.prompt: Why must transplant patients take immunosuppressant drugs?
answers: Otherwise the immune system rejects the foreign organ
wrong: To make the organ work faster
To avoid infection from the organ
questions.explanation: Tissue is matched by the HLA (MHC) type.

questions.prompt: What are the HLA (MHC) molecules on the surface of cells for?
answers: They show the T cells what is inside the cell, and mark it as 'self'
They present antigens to T cells
questions.explanation: Different in every person, apart from identical twins.

questions.prompt: What is the name for small proteins that immune cells use to talk to each other?
questions.explanation: Interleukins and interferons are examples.

questions.prompt: About what share of the white blood cells are lymphocytes?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are the most common type.

questions.prompt: What is a cancer of the lymphatic tissue, which can start in a lymph node, called?
questions.explanation: The two main kinds are Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
